C, C++, and Fortran allow arbitrary pointer arithmetic without bounds checking, which leaves them memory-unsafe [3].

Rust replaces classes and inheritance with structs, enums, traits, and methods [1].

{"result":"# The Rust Programming Language and Memory Safety

Rust is a general-purpose language that balances performance, type safety, and concurrency [1]. Memory safety, however, is its central promise, and it shapes much of its design.

Graydon Hoare began developing Rust in 2006, and Mozilla Research sponsored it from 2009 [2]. The language was first released publicly in 2010, with version 1.0 arriving in 2015 [2]. Its syntax resembles C++, yet it guarantees memory safety without a garbage collector [2]. Functional ideas such as pattern matching also shaped its design [1].

Memory safety protects programs from bugs such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. Java achieves this partly through runtime checks of array bounds and pointer dereferences [3]. By contrast, C, C++, and Fortran remain memory-unsafe [3].

Rust replaces classes and inheritance with structs, enums, traits, and methods [1]. For systems programmers, this design offers a practical trade-off: stricter rules during development in exchange for fewer memory errors at runtime.
